title: Vayigash: the wagons (Genesis 45:26–28)
hookLine: Jacob can't believe it until he sees the wagons, then his spirit revives
last: DON'T FALL OUT ON THE WAY.

lines: AN OLD MAN AND A BLOODY COAT.
cards: Some news is too good to believe. The phone call that says the test came back clear. The text from someone you thought you'd lost touch with forever.
Your first reaction isn't joy. It's: no, that can't be right. Now picture an old man who has grieved a son for over twenty years.
He was shown a bloody coat. He said he'd go down to his grave mourning. And his sons walk in and say: Joseph is alive.
He's the ruler of all Egypt.

teach.b: The first reaction, the text says, is that Jacob's heart went numb. He didn't believe them. Words weren't enough.
So the brothers tell him everything Joseph said.
Then he sees the wagons Joseph had sent from Egypt to carry him down. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "the spirit of Jacob their father revived." Then he speaks.
"It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive; I will go and see him before I die." Why the wagons? The rabbis noticed a pun.

teach.h: AGALOT — A SIGNAL FROM A SON.
teach.b: The Hebrew for wagons, agalot, sounds like eglah, a young cow.
Rashi passes on a tradition that the last thing Jacob and Joseph studied together, before Joseph vanished, was a passage about a heifer.
So the wagons were a private signal only a father would understand: it's really me, and I remember.
Later storytellers add a tender scene the Torah doesn't have: Asher's daughter, Serach, breaks the news to her grandfather gently, in a song, so the shock won't hurt him.
The Torah itself is silent about how they told him. And watch one small thing.
In the verse where his spirit revives, he's still Jacob. In the very next verse, when he decides to go, the text calls him Israel, his larger name.

Rashi adds that the presence of God, which had left him in his grief, came back. Sometimes good news needs to be seen before it can be believed. And sometimes the person delivering it matters as much as the news.

how: Jewish tradition has blessings for news: on hearing good news that benefits others too, many say the blessing praising God who is good and does good, and on hard news they say the blessing for the true Judge.

o: and he slept, the portion of Jacob's ladder dream
and he approached, the portion of Jacob's news
the tent, the portion where Abraham greets guests

games.q: how Jacob came to believe — tap the pairs.
p: wagons, sounds like a young cow
the name used once his spirit revives

s: Jacob believed his sons the moment they told him
his heart went numb and he didn't believe them, until he heard Joseph's words and saw the wagons.
the Torah describes Serach singing the news to Jacob
that scene comes from later storytellers. the Torah doesn't say how they told him.
the text switches from Jacob to Israel as he revives
after his spirit revives, verse 28 calls him Israel.

games.q: you're one of the brothers. your father doesn't believe that Joseph is alive. what do you do?
o: leave it, he'll believe it when he's ready.
tell him every word Joseph said, and show him the wagons.
admit everything about the sale first.
games.why: they told him all Joseph's words, and when he saw the wagons Joseph had sent, his spirit revived. the Torah never records them confessing the sale to him.

practice: Think of one piece of good news you're holding that someone else would love to hear: a thank-you you haven't passed on, a compliment said behind their back, their kid did well, the thing they worried about worked out.
Picture their face when they hear it, and decide how and when you'll tell them; sooner is kinder.

wordCard.voice: Vayigash. The portion where Jacob hears his lost son is alive, sees the wagons, and his spirit comes back to life.

orig.note: Hebrew: and the spirit of Jacob revived (Genesis 45:27).
